narrative: Fire ecology featured prominently today: work from Australia's Black Summer shows biodiversity-focused emergency response can be integrated into disaster management, while multi-decadal Pantanal data reveal that reduced precipitation and shrinking flood pulses have driven a marked shift toward larger, longer fire seasons since 2014. Climate change continues to reshape species distributions and phenology, from projected habitat loss for critically endangered commercial fish by 2100 to evidence that vegetation phenology actively compensates for, rather than simply responding to, drought extremes. On movement and behaviour, GPS tracking shows migratory red deer redistribute nitrogen across alpine elevational gradients, while a global meta-analysis finds urban wildlife—especially birds—consistently display bolder, more exploratory behaviour than rural counterparts. Invasion ecology contributions include evidence that one alien species can facilitate further invasions by reducing litter allelochemical defences, and an experimental demonstration that invasive goldfish trigger regime shifts in lake ecosystems regardless of starting trophic state. In methods, several new bioacoustic tools stood out, including a contrastive language-audio pretraining approach for global soundscape characterisation and a zero-shot classifier transferring frog-call recognition across continents, alongside a major software update extending the 'biomod2' species distribution modelling package. Conservation highlights include long-term recovery of mammal populations in subtropical China following reduced poaching pressure after an extreme ice storm, and successful vegetation recovery in rewetted temperate peatlands 38 years after forestry drainage ceased.
